idiom_name: abstract Command base + virtual execute() + Boost.Serialization / cereal polymorphic registration
implementation_notes: Virtual dispatch is native C++, so the Command half of the pattern is a small abstract base; the real work is serialising a polymorphic type. The classic realization derives commands from `Command`, declares `virtual void execute()`, gives the base a `serialize()` that writes the archive, and registers every concrete type with the archive (BOOST_CLASS_EXPORT, or cereal's CEREAL_REGISTER_TYPE plus CEREAL_REGISTER_POLYMORPHIC_RELATION) so the far side can reconstruct the derived type from the archive's class key. Registration may be static or done dynamically in the base's save/load pair; either way both sides need it. Exchange archives are versioned and registry-dependent, which is the price of runtime extensibility.
pitfalls: Without BOOST_CLASS_EXPORT (or cereal's registration macros in a header both sides include) loading through a base pointer throws "unregistered class", while static registration can drag otherwise-unused types into the binary.
Archive class keys are type names or GUIDs: renaming namespaces or classes silently breaks old queued messages, so pin explicit keys for anything durable.
Pointer graphs cannot cross the boundary - a command holding a receiver pointer must serialise the receiver's identity instead.

variants.name: Closed std::variant command set with visit dispatch and a tagged JSON/protobuf codec
variants.idiom_name: std::variant<...> + std::visit over a discriminated JSON/protobuf payload
variants.implementation_notes: The modern alternative removes runtime registration entirely: commands are plain structs in a closed `std::variant`, the wire form carries an explicit discriminator (a JSON tag field via nlohmann::json, or a protobuf oneof) and dispatch is `std::visit` or a tag switch, so adding a command means recompiling the variant - no archive keys, no per-type registration, no silent unknown-type failures. Choose it when the command set is known at compile time and both sides build together; the virtual-base variant stays justified when commands must be pluggable across binaries or carry behaviour that also runs in-process.
pitfalls: A closed variant set means a new command on the wire requires a redeploy of every consumer; unknown discriminators must be rejected explicitly into a dead-letter path.
std::visit dispatch and the JSON tag must stay in sync - derive the tag from one table, not from two hand-written switches.
